claim: Midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons have been thought to primarily encode reward prediction error (RPE).
source: Although midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons have been thought to primarily encode reward prediction error (RPE), recent studies have also found movement-related DAergic signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Recent studies have found movement-related dopaminergic signals.
source: Although midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons have been thought to primarily encode reward prediction error (RPE), recent studies have also found movement-related DAergic signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: DA neurons in mice projecting to dorsomedial striatum are modulated by choices contralateral to the recording side.
source: For example, we recently reported that DA neurons in mice projecting to dorsomedial striatum are modulated by choices contralateral to the recording side.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Parker et al., 2016).

claim: DA signals are modulated by contralateral choice in a manner that is distinct from RPE.
source: By considering both choice and RPE on a trial-by-trial basis, we find that DA signals are modulated by contralateral choice in a manner that is distinct from RPE, implying that choice encoding is better explained by movement direction.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Choice encoding in DMS-projecting DA neurons is better explained by movement direction than by RPE.
source: By considering both choice and RPE on a trial-by-trial basis, we find that DA signals are modulated by contralateral choice in a manner that is distinct from RPE, implying that choice encoding is better explained by movement direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing distinct modulation patterns.

claim: Manipulation of DA produces gross effects on movement initiation and invigoration.
source: Although manipulation of DA produces gross effects on movement initiation and invigoration, physiological recordings of DA neurons have historically shown few neural correlates of motor events (Wise, 2004; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Physiological recordings of DA neurons have historically shown few neural correlates of motor events.
source: Although manipulation of DA produces gross effects on movement initiation and invigoration, physiological recordings of DA neurons have historically shown few neural correlates of motor events (Wise, 2004; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic studies.

claim: Classic studies reported DA neuron responses to rewards and reward-predicting cues.
source: Instead, classic studies reported responses to rewards and reward-predicting cues, with a pattern suggesting that DA neurons carry a 'reward prediction error' (RPE) — the difference between expected reward and observed reward — for learning to anticipate rewards (Schultz et al., 1997; Barto, 1995; Cohen et al., 2012; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Soares et al., 2016; Hart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to classic and recent literature.

claim: DA neurons carry a reward prediction error (RPE) signal for learning to anticipate rewards.
source: Instead, classic studies reported responses to rewards and reward-predicting cues, with a pattern suggesting that DA neurons carry a 'reward prediction error' (RPE) — the difference between expected reward and observed reward — for learning to anticipate rewards (Schultz et al., 1997; Barto, 1995; Cohen et al., 2012; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Soares et al., 2016; Hart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: In the classic framework, DA neurons influence movements indirectly by determining which movements are learned and/or determining the general motivation to engage in a movement.
source: In this classic framework, rather than explicitly encoding movement, DA neurons influence movements indirectly by determining which movements are learned and/or determining the general motivation to engage in a movement (Niv et al., 2007; Collins and Frank, 2014; Berke, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical literature.

claim: Subpopulations of DA neurons may have a more direct role in encoding movement.
source: Complicating this classic view, however, several recent studies have suggested that subpopulations of DA neurons may have a more direct role in encoding movement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: DA neurons projecting to ventral striatum showed classic RPE signals.
source: For example, we recently reported that whereas DA neurons projecting to ventral striatum showed classic RPE signals, a subset of midbrain DA neurons that project to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) were selective for a mouse's choice of action (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: A subset of midbrain DA neurons that project to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) were selective for a mouse's choice of action.
source: For example, we recently reported that whereas DA neurons projecting to ventral striatum showed classic RPE signals, a subset of midbrain DA neurons that project to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) were selective for a mouse's choice of action (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: DMS-projecting DA neurons responded more strongly during contralateral (versus ipsilateral) choices as mice performed a probabilistic learning task.
source: In particular, they responded more strongly during contralateral (versus ipsilateral) choices as mice performed a probabilistic learning task (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Several recent studies reported phasic changes in DA activity at the onset of spontaneous movements.
source: In addition, there have been several other recent studies that reported phasic changes in DA activity at the onset of spontaneous movements (Dodson et al., 2016; Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Howe et al., 2013; da Silva et al., 2018; Barter et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: DA neurons may have signals related to novel or aversive stimuli.
source: Moreoever, other studies have shown that DA neurons may have other forms of apparently non-RPE signals, such as signals related to novel or aversive stimuli (Menegas et al., 2017; Horvitz, 2000; Ungless et al., 2004; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Lammel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature.

claim: Movement-related DA signals could influence movement via directly modulating striatal medium spiny neurons.
source: For instance, while it seems plausible that movement-related DA signals could influence movement via directly modulating striatal medium spiny neurons (DeLong, 1990), these signals are accompanied in the same recordings by RPEs which are thought to drive corticostriatal plasticity (Reynolds et al., 2001).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations.

claim: RPE signals are thought to drive corticostriatal plasticity.
source: For instance, while it seems plausible that movement-related DA signals could influence movement via directly modulating striatal medium spiny neurons (DeLong, 1990), these signals are accompanied in the same recordings by RPEs which are thought to drive corticostriatal plasticity (Reynolds et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Computational models like advantage learning and actor-critic learn separate predictions about the overall value of situations and about the value of specific actions.
source: Specifically, computational models like advantage learning (Baird, 1994) and actor-critic (Barto et al., 1983) learn separate predictions about the overall value of situations or stimuli and about the value of specific actions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational modeling literature.

claim: It has been suggested that overall value and action-specific value calculations might be localized to ventral vs dorsal striatum respectively.
source: It has long been suggested these two calculations might be localized to ventral vs dorsal striatum respectively (Montague et al., 1996; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: A human neuroimaging experiment reported evidence of distinct prediction errors for right and left movements in the corresponding contralateral striatum.
source: Furthermore, a human neuroimaging experiment reported evidence of distinct prediction errors for right and left movements in the corresponding contralateral striatum (Gershman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a neuroimaging study.

claim: A choice-specific RPE could explain choice-related correlates observed prior to the time of reward.
source: Importantly, a choice-specific RPE could explain choice-related correlates observed prior to the time of reward.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about how RPE signals work.

claim: Temporal difference RPEs have a phasic anticipatory component triggered by predictive cues indicating the availability and timing of future reward.
source: This is because temporal difference RPEs do not just signal error when a reward is received, they also have a phasic anticipatory component triggered by predictive cues indicating the availability and timing of future reward, such as (in choice tasks) the presentation of levers or choice targets (Montague et al., 1996; Morris et al., 2006; Roesch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on temporal difference learning.

claim: The anticipatory prediction error is proportional to the value of the future expected reward following a given choice.
source: This anticipatory prediction error is proportional to the value of the future expected reward following a given choice — indeed, we henceforth refer to this component of the RPE as a 'value' signal, which tracks the reward expected for a choice.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of temporal difference learning theory.

claim: A choice-specific value signal can masquerade as a choice signal because animals are more likely to choose actions that they predict have high value.
source: Crucially, a choice-specific value signal can masquerade as a choice signal because, by definition, action and value are closely related to each other: animals are more likely to choose actions that they predict have high value.
evidence: This is based on inference from decision theory and supported by citation.

claim: A value signal (RPE) for the contralateral choice will tend to be larger when that action is chosen than when it is not.
source: In this case, a value signal (RPE) for the contralateral choice will tend to be larger when that action is chosen than when it is not (Samuelson, 1938).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to economic theory.

claim: DMS-projecting DA neurons' signals are modulated by value (RPE).
source: Ultimately, our results show that DMS-projecting DA neurons' signals are indeed modulated by value (RPE), but, crucially, this modulation reflected the value of the chosen action rather than the contralateral one.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The value modulation in DMS-projecting DA neurons reflected the value of the chosen action rather than the contralateral one.
source: Ultimately, our results show that DMS-projecting DA neurons' signals are indeed modulated by value (RPE), but, crucially, this modulation reflected the value of the chosen action rather than the contralateral one.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The value aspects of DMS-projecting DA signals could not explain the contralateral choice selectivity in these neurons.
source: Thus, the value aspects of the signals (which were not lateralized) could not explain the contralateral choice selectivity in these neurons, implying that this choice-dependent modulation indeed reflects modulation by contralateral movements and not value.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing distinct patterns of value and movement modulation.

claim: The choice-dependent modulation in DMS-projecting DA neurons reflects modulation by contralateral movements and not value.
source: Thus, the value aspects of the signals (which were not lateralized) could not explain the contralateral choice selectivity in these neurons, implying that this choice-dependent modulation indeed reflects modulation by contralateral movements and not value.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: Mice were trained on a probabilistic reversal learning task.
source: Mice were trained on a probabilistic reversal learning task as reported previously (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Each trial began with an illumination in the nose port, which cued the mouse to initiate a nose poke.
source: Each trial began with an illumination in the nose port, which cued the mouse to initiate a nose poke (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure and is shown in Figure 1a.

claim: After a 0–1 second delay, two levers appeared on both sides of the nose port.
source: After a 0–1 second delay, two levers appeared on both sides of the nose port.
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure.

claim: Each lever led to reward either with high probability (70%) or low probability (10%).
source: Each lever led to reward either with high probability (70%) or low probability (10%), with the identity of the high probability lever swapping after a block of variable length (see Materials and methods for more details, Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure and is shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The identity of the high probability lever swapped after a block of variable length.
source: Each lever led to reward either with high probability (70%) or low probability (10%), with the identity of the high probability lever swapping after a block of variable length (see Materials and methods for more details, Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure.

claim: After another 0–1 second delay, the mouse either received a sucrose reward and an accompanying auditory stimulus (positive conditioned stimulus, or CS+), or no reward and a different auditory stimulus (negative conditioned stimulus, or CS-).
source: After another 0–1 second delay, the mouse either received a sucrose reward and an accompanying auditory stimulus (positive conditioned stimulus, or CS+), or no reward and a different auditory stimulus (negative conditioned stimulus, or CS-).
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure.

claim: Mice gradually learned to prefer the lever with the higher chance of reward after each transition.
source: Given that block transitions were not signaled to the mouse, mice gradually learned to prefer the lever with the higher chance of reward after each transition.
evidence: This is observed from the behavioral data.

claim: A trial-by-trial Q-learning model was fit to predict the probability of the animal's choice at each trial of the task.
source: To capture this learning, we fit their choices using a standard trial-by-trial Q-learning model that predicted the probability of the animal's choice at each trial of the task (Figure 1c, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach used.

claim: Activity was recorded from either the terminals or cell bodies of DA neurons that project to DMS (VTA/SN::DMS) using fiber photometry to measure the fluorescence of the calcium indicator GCaMP6f.
source: As mice performed this task, we recorded activity from either the terminals or cell bodies of DA neurons that project to DMS (VTA/SN::DMS) using fiber photometry to measure the fluorescence of the calcium indicator GCaMP6f (Figure 1d,e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This describes the recording methods used.

claim: VTA/SN::DMS neurons revealed elevated activity during contralateral choice trials relative to ipsilateral choice trials, particularly in relation to the nose poke and lever presentation events.
source: As previously reported, this revealed elevated activity during contralateral choice trials relative to ipsilateral choice trials, particularly in relation to the nose poke and lever presentation events (Figure 1f,g; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the figures and citation to previous work.

claim: If neurons in DMS participate in contralateral movements, a side-specific error signal would be appropriate for teaching them when those movements are valuable.
source: The motivation for this hypothesis is that, if neurons in DMS participate in contralateral movements, such a side-specific error signal would be appropriate for teaching them when those movements are valuable.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about learning mechanisms.

claim: If DA neurons display contralateral value modulation, the relative value of the contralateral (versus ipsilateral) choice modulates DA signals, regardless of whether the choice is contralateral or ipsilateral.
source: In this case, the relative value of the contralateral (versus ipsilateral) choice modulates DA signals, regardless of whether the choice is contralateral or ipsilateral.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about how contralateral value modulation would manifest.

claim: Under contralateral value modulation, the direction of value modulation would depend on the choice: signals are highest for contralateral choices when these are relatively most valuable, but lowest for ipsilateral choices when they are most valuable.
source: Thus, when the DA signals are broken down with respect to both the action chosen and its value, the direction of value modulation would depend on the choice: signals are highest for contralateral choices when these are relatively most valuable, but lowest for ipsilateral choices when they are most valuable (because in this case, contralateral choices will be relatively less valuable).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: Assuming mice tend to choose the option they expect to deliver more reward, contralateral value signals would be larger, on average, during contralateral choices than ipsilateral ones.
source: Assuming mice tend to choose the option they expect to deliver more reward, such signals would be larger, on average, during contralateral choices than ipsilateral ones (Figure 2a), which could in theory explain the contralateral choice selectivity that we observed (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is an inference based on decision theory and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: Chosen value modulation corresponds to the standard type of 'critic' RPE most often invoked in models of DA.
source: This corresponds to the standard type of 'critic' RPE most often invoked in models of DA: that is, RPE with respect to the overall value of the current state or situation (where that state reflects any choices previously made), and not specialized to a particular class of action.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of reinforcement learning theory.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies have primarily reported correlates of the value of the chosen option in DA target areas.
source: Indeed, human neuroimaging studies have primarily reported correlates of the value of the chosen option in DA target areas (Daw et al., 2006; Boorman et al., 2009; Li and Daw, 2011), and this also has been observed in primate DA neurons (Morris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: Chosen value modulation has been observed in primate DA neurons.
source: Indeed, human neuroimaging studies have primarily reported correlates of the value of the chosen option in DA target areas (Daw et al., 2006; Boorman et al., 2009; Li and Daw, 2011), and this also has been observed in primate DA neurons (Morris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to primate electrophysiology literature.

claim: If DMS-projecting DA neurons display chosen value modulation, the value modulation for both contralateral and ipsilateral choices would be similar.
source: If DMS-projecting DA neurons indeed display chosen value modulation (Figure 2b), rather than contralateral value modulation, the value modulation for both contralateral and ipsilateral choices would be similar.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: If DMS-projecting DA neurons display chosen value modulation, value modulation could not in itself account for the neurons' elevated activity during contralateral trials.
source: In this case, value modulation could not in itself account for the neurons' elevated activity during contralateral trials, which we have previously observed (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model.

claim: To account for contralateral choice preference under chosen value modulation, one would have to assume DA neurons are also selective for the contralateral action itself (unrelated to their value modulation).
source: Therefore, to account for contralateral choice preference, one would have to assume DA neurons are also selective for the contralateral action itself (unrelated to their value modulation; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model illustrated in Figure 2c.

claim: VTA/SN::DMS terminals were modulated by the previous trial's reward.
source: The traces (Figure 3a) indicated that the VTA/SN::DMS terminals were modulated by the previous trial's reward.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The value-related signals in VTA/SN::DMS terminals reflected chosen value — responding more when the previous choice was rewarded, whether contralateral or ipsilateral.
source: The value-related signals reflected chosen value — responding more when the previous choice was rewarded, whether contralateral or ipsilateral — and therefore did not explain the movement-related effect.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The value-related signals in VTA/SN::DMS terminals did not explain the movement-related effect.
source: The value-related signals reflected chosen value — responding more when the previous choice was rewarded, whether contralateral or ipsilateral — and therefore did not explain the movement-related effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: DMS-projecting DA neurons represented both chosen value and movement direction.
source: This indicated that the DMS-projecting DA neurons represented both chosen value and movement direction (similar to Figure 2c).
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: The effect of contralateral action modulation was visible in individual, non-z-scored data in both VTA/SN::DMS terminals and VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies.
source: The effect of contralateral action modulation was also visible in individual, non-z-scored data in both VTA/SN::DMS terminals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Binning trials by chosen (minus unchosen) value revealed a movement effect and value gradient.
source: Binning trials by chosen (minus unchosen) value, a similar movement effect and value gradient emerged as we have seen with the previous trial outcome analysis (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Trials with higher Q values had larger GCaMP6f signals, regardless which side was chosen.
source: Trials with higher Q values had larger GCaMP6f signals, regardless which side was chosen, again suggesting that VTA/SN::DMS terminals were modulated by the expected value of the chosen (not contralateral) action, in addition to being modulated by contralateral movement.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: VTA/SN::DMS terminals were modulated by the expected value of the chosen (not contralateral) action, in addition to being modulated by contralateral movement.
source: Trials with higher Q values had larger GCaMP6f signals, regardless which side was chosen, again suggesting that VTA/SN::DMS terminals were modulated by the expected value of the chosen (not contralateral) action, in addition to being modulated by contralateral movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: Linear mixed effects regression verified significant effects for both movement direction and action value.
source: The results verify significant effects for both movement direction and action value; that is, although a significant value effect is seen, it does not explain away the movement effect.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The significant value effect does not explain away the movement effect in DMS-projecting DA neurons.
source: The results verify significant effects for both movement direction and action value; that is, although a significant value effect is seen, it does not explain away the movement effect.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis.

claim: There is a small interaction between the variables earlier in the trial, before 0.25 seconds, reflecting small differences in the magnitude of value modulation on contralateral versus ipsilateral trials.
source: (There is a small interaction between the variables earlier in the trial, before 0.25 seconds, reflecting small differences in the magnitude of value modulation on contralateral versus ipsilateral trials.)
evidence: This is observed in the statistical analysis.

claim: When the regression is re-estimated in terms of contralateral value rather than chosen value, a sustained, significant interaction emerges.
source: Conversely, when the regression is re-estimated in terms of contralateral value rather than chosen value, a sustained, significant interaction does emerge, providing formal statistical support for the chosen value model; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Very similar modulation by both chosen value and contralateral movement was found in both VTA/SN::DMS cell bodies and terminals.
source: We performed the same value modulation analyses on the cell bodies, rather than terminals, of VTA/SN::DMS neurons (Figure 3d–f). This was motivated by the possibility that there may be changes in neural coding between DA cell bodies and terminals due to direct activation of DA terminals. In this case, we found very similar modulation by both chosen value and contralateral movement in both recording locations.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: The same basic pattern of effects was found when analyses were repeated on DA signals time-locked to nose poke event.
source: First, we repeated our analyses on DA signals time-locked to nose poke event (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and found the same basic pattern of effects.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The effect was clearest close to the average lever presentation latency, suggesting that the modulation of DA signals is more closely related to lever presentation.
source: The effect was still clearest close to the average lever presentation latency, suggesting that the modulation of DA signals is more closely related to lever presentation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: A linear regression model with kernels capturing the contribution of three different events (Nose Poke, Lever Presentation, and Lever Press) simultaneously produced results consistent with the simpler single-event regression.
source: To more directly verify that our conclusions are independent of the specific choice event alignment, we fit a linear regression model with kernels capturing the contribution of three different events (Nose Poke, Lever Presentation, and Lever Press) simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The results of this multiple event regression were consistent with the simpler single-event regression in Figure 3a,d.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The side-specific effects reversed within animal when comparing signals across hemispheres in individual mice.
source: Taking advantage of the fact that the VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies data had recordings from both hemispheres in three animals, we directly compared signals across hemispheres in individual mice and observed that the side-specific effects reversed within animal (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The reversal of side-specific effects within animal speaks against the possibility that they might reflect animal-specific idiosyncrasies such as side biases.
source: This speaks against the possibility that they might reflect animal-specific idiosyncrasies such as side biases.
evidence: This is inferred from the within-animal comparison.

claim: Lever-press latency was not a strong predictor for GCaMP6f signals in both VTA/SN::DMS terminals and cell-bodies.
source: For both VTA/SN::DMS terminals and cell-bodies data, the lever-press latency was not a strong predictor for GCaMP6f signals, and the effect of the original predictors largely remained the same (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: When signals were time-locked to the lever press itself, there was a reversal of the signal selectivity between contralateral and ipsilateral trials, shortly after the lever press.
source: When the signals were time-locked to the lever press itself, there was a reversal of the signal selectivity between contralateral and ipsilateral trials, shortly after the lever press (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reversal in signal selectivity at lever press coincided with a reversal in the animal's physical movement direction.
source: Although body tracking is not available, this event coincided with a reversal in the animal's physical movement direction, from moving towards the lever from the central nosepoke before the lever press, to moving back to the central reward port after the lever press.
evidence: This is inferred from the task structure, though body tracking data is not available.

claim: There is no reversal in value modulation at the time of lever press.
source: In contrast, there is no reversal in value modulation at the time of lever press.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fact that the side-specific modulation (and not the value modulation) followed the mice's movement direction during the trial further indicated that movement direction explains the choice selectivity in these DA neurons.
source: The fact that the side-specific modulation (and not the value modulation) followed the mice's movement direction during the trial further indicated that movement direction explains the choice selectivity in these DA neurons, and resists explanation in terms of RPE-related signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: The choice selectivity in DMS-projecting DA neurons resists explanation in terms of RPE-related signaling.
source: The fact that the side-specific modulation (and not the value modulation) followed the mice's movement direction during the trial further indicated that movement direction explains the choice selectivity in these DA neurons, and resists explanation in terms of RPE-related signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence clearly indicated that DMS-projecting DA neurons contain distinct movement- and value-related signals, tied to different frames of reference.
source: To investigate this possibility, we dissected movement direction and value selectivity in the signals of terminals and cell bodies of DMS-projecting DA neurons (Figure 3). Contrary to the hypothesis that lateralized movement-related activity might reflect a RPE for contralateral value, multiple lines of evidence clearly indicated that the neurons instead contain distinct movement- and value-related signals, tied to different frames of reference.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the data analyses.

claim: Value-related signals preceding and following the lever press were observed in DMS-projecting DA neurons, which are consistent with the anticipatory component of a classic RPE signal.
source: We did observe value-related signals preceding and following the lever press, which we did not previously analyze in the DMS signal and which are consistent with the anticipatory component of a classic RPE signal (Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citation to previous work.

claim: Because value-related signals were modulated by the value of the chosen action, not the contralateral one, they cannot explain the side-specific movement selectivity.
source: But because these were modulated by the value of the chosen action, not the contralateral one, they cannot explain the side-specific movement selectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis.

claim: The movement and value signals showed clearly distinct time courses.
source: The two signals also showed clearly distinct time courses; in particular, the side selectivity reversed polarity following the lever press, but value modulation did not.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The side selectivity reversed polarity following the lever press, but value modulation did not.
source: The two signals also showed clearly distinct time courses; in particular, the side selectivity reversed polarity following the lever press, but value modulation did not.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Syed et al. recently reported that DA release in the nucleus accumbens (NAcc) was elevated during 'go', rather than 'no-go', responses, alongside classic RPE-related signals.
source: For example, Syed et al. recently reported that DA release in the nucleus accumbens (NAcc) was elevated during 'go', rather than 'no-go', responses, alongside classic RPE-related signals (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claim: NAcc may have parallel movement-specific and chosen value signals.
source: There is at least a hint (albeit significant only at one timepoint in Syed et al.'s Supplemental Figure 9E) that it does not do so (Syed et al., 2016). This suggests that NAcc may also have parallel movement-specific and chosen value signals, which would be broadly confirmatory for our parallel conclusions about DMS-projecting DA neurons.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on reinterpretation of another study's data.

claim: The RPE account of the DA signal proposes that the system's reward-related signals ultimately affect movement indirectly, either by driving learning about movement direction preferences or by modulating motivation to act.
source: The RPE account of the DA signal has long held out hope for a unifying perspective on the system's dual roles in movement and reward by proposing that the system's reward-related signals ultimately affect movement indirectly, either by driving learning about movement direction preferences (Montague et al., 1996) or by modulating motivation to act (Niv et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical literature.

claim: The RPE theory accounts for multiple seemingly distinct components of the classic DA signal, including anticipatory and reward-related signals, and signals to novel neutral cues.
source: This RPE theory also accounts for multiple seemingly distinct components of the classic DA signal, including anticipatory and reward-related signals, and signals to novel neutral cues.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of RPE theory.

claim: The present analyses clearly show that side-specific signals in DMS resist explanation in terms of an extended RPE account.
source: However, the present analyses clearly show that side-specific signals in DMS resist explanation in terms of an extended RPE account, and may instead simply reflect planned or ongoing movements.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the data analyses.

claim: Side-specific signals in DMS may simply reflect planned or ongoing movements.
source: However, the present analyses clearly show that side-specific signals in DMS resist explanation in terms of an extended RPE account, and may instead simply reflect planned or ongoing movements.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The results are consistent with the longstanding suggestion that DA signals may be important for directly initiating movement.
source: Specifically, our results are consistent with the longstanding suggestion that DA signals may be important for directly initiating movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in light of existing theory.

claim: Movement-related DA signals may elicit or execute contralateral movements via differentially modulating the direct and indirect pathways out of the striatum.
source: Such a signal may elicit or execute contralateral movements via differentially modulating the direct and indirect pathways out of the striatum (Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Collins and Frank, 2014; DeLong, 1990).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations.

claim: Unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) lesions increase ipsilateral rotations.
source: For instance, classic results demonstrate that unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) lesions increase ipsilateral rotations (Costall et al., 1976; Ungerstedt and Arbuthnott, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic lesion studies.

claim: Unilateral optogenetic excitation of midbrain DA neurons in mice led to contralateral rotations developed over the course of days.
source: Consistent with those results, a recent study reports that unilateral optogenetic excitation of midbrain DA neurons in mice led to contralateral rotations developed over the course of days (Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent optogenetic study.

claim: The results are correlational, and cannot rule out the possibility that the particular activity studied could be related to a range of functions other than movement execution, such as planning or monitoring.
source: Importantly, however, our own results are correlational, and we cannot rule out the possibility that the particular activity we study could be related to a range of functions other than movement execution, such as planning or monitoring.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: The main result is to rule out the possibility that neural activity is better accounted for by the motivational variable of predicted value.
source: Although motivation is a broad concept and difficult to operationalize fully, our results address two aspects of it. First, one way to quantify the motivation to act is by the action's predicted value; thus, our main result is to rule out the possibility that neural activity is better accounted for by this motivational variable.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Lever press latency does not explain the contralateralized DA signals.
source: We also show that lever press latency (arguably another proxy for motivation) does not explain the contralateralized DA signals (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: It is unclear how recipient synapses would distinguish an RPE component of the DA signal from an overlapping component more relevant to movement elicitation.
source: Although the movement-related DA signal might be appropriate for execution, it is less clear how it might interact with the plasticity mechanisms hypothesized to be modulated by RPE aspects of the DA signal (Frank et al., 2004; Steinberg et al., 2013; Reynolds and Wickens, 2002). For instance, how would recipient synapses distinguish an RPE component of the signal (appropriate for surprise-modulated learning) from an overlapping component more relevant to movement elicitation (Berke, 2018)?
evidence: This is a theoretical question raised by the findings.

claim: Plasticity in the dorsal striatum itself may follow different rules, which might require an action rather than a prediction error signal.
source: One possibility is that plasticity in the dorsal striatum itself follows different rules, which might require an action rather than a prediction error signal (Saunders et al., 2018; Yttri and Dudman, 2016)
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations.

claim: Some types of instrumental learning are correlational rather than error-driven.
source: For instance, it has been suggested that some types of instrumental learning are correlational rather than error-driven (Doeller et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: An early model of instrumental learning posits that stimulus-response habits are not learned from an action's rewarding consequences, but instead by directly memorizing which actions the organism tends to select in a situation.
source: and, more specifically, an early model of instrumental learning (Guthrie, 1935) recently revived by (Miller et al., 2019) posits that stimulus-response habits are not learned from an action's rewarding consequences, as in RPE models, but instead by directly memorizing which actions the organism tends to select in a situation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical literature.

claim: The results point to the need for an extended computational account that incorporates the movement direction signals as well as the RPE ones.
source: Overall, our results point to the need for an extended computational account that incorporates the movement direction signals as well as the RPE ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings.

claim: Lateralized movement selectivity tracks choices contralateral versus ipsilateral of the recorded hemisphere.
source: Lateralized movement selectivity tracks choices contralateral versus ipsilateral of the recorded hemisphere — appropriate for motor control — but the value component instead relates to the reward expected for the chosen, versus unchosen, action.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: The value component in DMS-projecting DA neurons relates to the reward expected for the chosen, versus unchosen, action.
source: Lateralized movement selectivity tracks choices contralateral versus ipsilateral of the recorded hemisphere — appropriate for motor control — but the value component instead relates to the reward expected for the chosen, versus unchosen, action.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Value modulation by the chosen action is suitable for a classic RPE for learning 'state' values.
source: This value modulation by the chosen action is suitable for a classic RPE for learning 'state' values (since overall value expectancy at any point in time is conditioned on the choices the animal has made; Morris et al., 2006), and also consistent with the bulk of BOLD signals in human neuroimaging, where value-related responding throughout DAergic targets tends to be organized on chosen-vs-unchosen lines (Daw et al., 2006; Boorman et al., 2009; Li and Daw, 2011; O'Doherty, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Value-related responding throughout DAergic targets in human neuroimaging tends to be organized on chosen-vs-unchosen lines.
source: This value modulation by the chosen action is suitable for a classic RPE for learning 'state' values (since overall value expectancy at any point in time is conditioned on the choices the animal has made; Morris et al., 2006), and also consistent with the bulk of BOLD signals in human neuroimaging, where value-related responding throughout DAergic targets tends to be organized on chosen-vs-unchosen lines (Daw et al., 2006; Boorman et al., 2009; Li and Daw, 2011; O'Doherty, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: Distinct action-specific error signals would be useful for learning about different actions or types of predictions.
source: At the same time, there have been persistent suggestions that given the high dimensionality of an organism's action space, distinct action-specific error signals would be useful for learning about different actions (Russell and Zimdars, 2003; Frank and Badre, 2012; Diuk et al., 2013) or types of predictions (Gardner et al., 2018; Lau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical literature.

claim: There is evidence from BOLD neuroimaging for contralateral error and value signals in the human brain.
source: Along these lines, there is evidence from BOLD neuroimaging for contralateral error and value signals in the human brain (Gershman et al., 2009; Palminteri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The decomposition of error signals remains an important possibility for future work aimed at understanding heterogeneity of DA signals.
source: Although the current study finds no evidence for such laterally decomposed RPEs in DMS, the decomposition of error signals remains an important possibility for future work aimed at understanding heterogeneity of DA signals, including other anomalous features like ramps (Howe et al., 2013; Berke, 2018; Gershman, 2014; Hamid et al., 2016; Engelhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies have shown that midbrain DA neurons may encode a range of behavioral variables, such as the mice's position, their velocity, their view-angle, and the accuracy of their performance.
source: Recent studies, for instance, have shown that midbrain DA neurons may also encode a range of behavioral variables, such as the mice's position, their velocity, their view-angle, and the accuracy of their performance (da Silva et al., 2018; Howe et al., 2013 Engelhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The modeling framework provides a way to understand how DA signals might be interpreted in different reference frames and how they might encode some form of RPEs with respect to different behavioral variables.
source: Our modeling provides a framework for understanding how these DA signals might be interpreted in different reference frames and how they might ultimately encode some form of RPEs with respect to different behavioral variables in the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the modeling approach.

claim: The results were consistent across both recording sites with DMS-projecting DA neurons: the cell bodies and the terminals.
source: Interestingly, our results were consistent across both recording sites with DMS-projecting DA neurons: the cell bodies and the terminals (Figure 3d–f, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the figures.

claim: The movement selectivity is not introduced in DA neurons at the terminal level.
source: This indicates that the movement selectivity is not introduced in DA neurons at the terminal level, for example via striatal cholinergic interneurons or glutamatergic inputs (Kosillo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of results across cell bodies and terminals.

claim: The use of fiber photometry assesses bulk GCaMP6f signals at the recording site rather than resolving individual neurons.
source: An important limitation of the study is the use of fiber photometry, which assesses bulk GCaMP6f signals at the recording site rather than resolving individual neurons.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: It remains possible that individual neurons do not multiplex the two signals observed, and that they are instead segregated between distinct populations.
source: Thus it remains possible that individual neurons do not multiplex the two signals we observe, and that they are instead segregated between distinct populations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an alternative interpretation given the methodological limitations.

claim: Future work should use higher resolution methods to examine these questions at the level of individual DA neurons.
source: Future work should use higher resolution methods to examine these questions at the level of individual DA neurons.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The reversal in selectivity seen in Figure 4 is inferred to reflect a change in movement direction, but head tracking would be required to verify this more directly.
source: A related limitation of this study is the relatively coarse behavioral monitoring; notably, we infer that the reversal in selectivity seen in Figure 4 reflects a change in movement direction, but head tracking would be required to verify this more directly.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation and inference.

claim: Future work with finer instrumentation could usefully dissect signal components related to finer-grained movements, and examine how these are related to (or dissociated from) value signals.
source: More generally, future work with finer instrumentation could usefully dissect signal components related to finer-grained movements, and examine how these are related to (or dissociated from) value signals.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: 17 male mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the tyrosine hydroxylase promoter (ThIRES-Cre) were used for the study.
source: This article reports on data from 17 male mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the tyrosine hydroxylase promoter (ThIRES-Cre), from which GCaMP6f recordings were obtained from DA neurons via fiber photometry.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: For DA terminal recordings, Cre-dependent GCaMP6f virus was injected into the VTA/SNc, and fibers were placed in the DMS.
source: In the case of DA terminal recordings, Cre-dependent GCaMP6f virus (AAV5-CAG-Flex-GCamp6f-WPRE-SV40; UPenn virus core, 500nL, titer of 3.53 × 1012 pp ml) was injected into the VTA/SNc, and fibers were placed in the DMS (M–L ± 1.5, A–P 0.74 and D–V −2.4 mm), with one recording area per mouse (n = 12 recording sites).
evidence: This describes the surgical methods for terminal recordings.

claim: For VTA/SN::DMS cell body recordings, Cre-dependent GCaMP6f virus was injected into the DMS, and fibers were placed on the cell bodies in VTA/SNc.
source: In the case of VTA/SN::DMS cell body recordings, Cre-dependent GCaMP6f virus (AAV5-CAG-Flex-GCamp6f-WPRE-SV40; UPenn virus core, 500nL, titer of 3.53 × 1012 pp ml) was injected into the DMS, and fibers were placed on the cell bodies in VTA/SNc (M–L ± 1.4, A–P 0.74, D–V −2.6 mm) to enable recordings from retrogradely labeled cells (n = 4 mice).
evidence: This describes the surgical methods for cell body recordings.

claim: Three of the mice were recorded from both hemispheres, providing a total of n = 7 recording sites for cell body recordings.
source: Three of the mice were recorded from both hemispheres, providing a total of n = 7 recording sites.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: One mouse was used for the GFP recordings as a control condition for VTA/SNc::DMS terminals recordings.
source: One mouse was used for the GFP recordings as a control condition for VTA/SNc::DMS terminals recordings (Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes the control experiment.

claim: The mouse had 10 seconds to press a lever after lever presentation, otherwise the trial was classified as an abandoned trial and excluded from analysis.
source: The mouse then had 10 seconds to press a lever, otherwise the trial was classified as an abandoned trial and excluded from analysis (this amounted to <2% of trials for all mice).
evidence: This describes the task structure and data exclusion criteria.

claim: Abandoned trials amounted to <2% of trials for all mice.
source: The mouse then had 10 seconds to press a lever, otherwise the trial was classified as an abandoned trial and excluded from analysis (this amounted to <2% of trials for all mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral data.

claim: Reward outcomes were accompanied by different auditory stimuli: 0.5 seconds of white noise for CS- and 0.5 seconds of 5 kHz pure tone for CS+.
source: Reward outcomes were accompanied by different auditory stimul: 0.5 seconds of white noise for CS- and 0.5 seconds of 5 kHz pure tone for CS+.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Every trial ended with a 3 seconds inter-trial delay.
source: Every trial ended with a 3 seconds inter-trial delay (after the CS- auditory stimulus or the mice exit the reward port).
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Each block consisted of at least 10 rewarded trials plus a random number of trials drawn from a Geometric distribution of p=0.4 (mean 2.5).
source: For the reversal learning, each of the levers either had a high probability for reward (70%) or low probability for reward (10%). Throughout the session, the identity of the high probability lever changed in a pseudorandom schedule; specifically, each block consisted of at least 10 rewarded trials plus a random number of trials drawn from a Geometric distribution of p=0.4 (mean 2.5).
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: On average, there were 23.23 ± 7.93 trials per block and 9.67 ± 3.66 blocks per session.
source: On average, there were 23.23 ± 7.93 trials per block and 9.67 ± 3.66 blocks per session.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral data.

claim: All fiber photometry recordings were acquired at 15 Hz.
source: All fiber photometry recordings were acquired at 15 Hz.
evidence: This describes the recording parameters.

claim: 2–6 recording sessions were obtained per recording site (one session/day), and these recordings were concatenated across session for all analyses.
source: 2–6 recording sessions were obtained per recording site (one session/day), and these recordings were concatenated across session for all analyses.
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure.

claim: On average, there were 1307.0 ± 676.01 trials per mouse.
source: On average, we had 1307.0 ± 676.01 trials per mouse (858.09 ± 368.56 trials per mouse for VTA/SN::DMS Terminals recordings and 448.91 ± 455.61 trials per mouse for VTA/SN::DMS Cell-bodies recordings).
evidence: This is a quantitative result describing the dataset.

claim: The signals from each recording site were post-processed with a high-pass FIR filter with a passband of 0.375 Hz, stopband of 0.075 Hz, and a stopband attenuation of 10 dB.
source: The signals from each recording site were post-processed with a high-pass FIR filter with a passband of 0.375 Hz, stopband of 0.075 Hz, and a stopband attenuation of 10 dB to remove baseline fluorescence and correct drift in baseline.
evidence: This describes the signal processing methods.

claim: dF/F was derived by dividing the high-pass filtered signal by the mean of the signal before high-pass filtering.
source: We derived dF/F by dividing the high-pass filtered signal by the mean of the signal before high-pass filtering.
evidence: This describes the signal processing methods.

claim: dF/F was z-scored for each recording site, with the mean and standard error calculated for the entire recording from each site.
source: We then z-scored dF/F for each recording site, with the the mean and standard error calculated for the entire recording from each site.
evidence: This describes the signal processing methods.

claim: The VTA/SN::DMS terminals data consisted of 10108 total trials across 12 recording sites.
source: The VTA/SN::DMS terminals data consisted of 10108 total trials across 12 recording sites, and VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies consisted of 4938 total trials across 7 recording sites.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the dataset.

claim: VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies data consisted of 4938 total trials across 7 recording sites.
source: The VTA/SN::DMS terminals data consisted of 10108 total trials across 12 recording sites, and VTA/SN::DMS cell-bodies consisted of 4938 total trials across 7 recording sites.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the dataset.

claim: The three free parameters of the Q-learning model were estimated separately for each subject, but jointly in a hierarchical random effects model.
source: The three free parameters of the model were estimated separately for each subject, but jointly (in a hierarchical random effects model) with group-level mean and variance parameters reflecting the distribution, over the population, of each subject-level parameter.
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: The parameters were estimated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, as implemented in the Stan programming language (version 2.17.1.0).
source: The parameters were estimated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, as implemented in the Stan programming language (version 2.17.1.0; Carpenter et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the computational methods.

claim: The model was run with 4 chains of 1000 iterations each (of which the first 250 were discarded for burn-in), and the parameter adapt_delta set to 0.99.
source: We ran the model with 4 chains of 1000 iterations for each (of which the first 250 were discarded for burn-in), and the parameter adapt_delta set to 0.99.
evidence: This describes the computational methods.

claim: Convergence was verified by visual inspection and by verifying that the potential scale reduction statistic Rhat was close to 1.0 (<0.003 for all parameters).
source: We verified convergence by visual inspection and by verifying that the potential scale reduction statistic Rhat (Gelman and Rubin, 1992) was close to 1.0 (<0.003 for all parameters) (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the model validation procedure.

claim: A linear mixed effect model regression was performed to predict GCaMP6f signal at each time point based on Q-values, choice (contralateral vs ipsilateral), their interaction, and an intercept.
source: In Figure 3c,f, we performed a linear mixed effect model regression to predict GCaMP6f signal at each time point based on Q-values, choice (contralateral vs ipsilateral), their interaction, and an intercept.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: The difference in Q values for the chosen vs unchosen levers was standardized for each mouse and each recording site.
source: We took the difference in Q values for the chosen vs unchosen levers, then we standardized the difference in Q values for each mouse and each recording site.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing for the regression.

claim: GCaMP6f was time-locked to lever presentation, regressing to data points 1 second before and 2 seconds after the time-locked event for 45 total regressions.
source: GCaMP6f was time-locked to lever presentation, regressing to data points 1 second before and 2 seconds after the time-locked event for 45 total regressions.
evidence: This describes the regression analysis procedure.

claim: The regression and calculation of p values was performed with the MixedModels package in Julia.
source: The regression, as well as the calculation of p values, was performed with the MixedModels package in Julia (Bezanson et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the statistical software used.

claim: The p values were corrected for false discovery rate over the ensemble of timepoints for each regression variable separately, using the procedure of Benjamini and Hochberg.
source: The p values were corrected for false discovery rate over the ensemble of timepoints for each regression variable separately, using the procedure of Benjamini and Hochberg (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) via the MultipleTesting package in Julia (Bezanson et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the statistical correction procedure.

claim: A linear regression model was fit to determine the contributions to the ongoing GCaMP6f signal of three simultaneously modeled events (nose poke, lever presentation, lever press) using kernels.
source: In Figure 3—figure supplement 5, we fit a linear regression model to determine the contributions to the ongoing GCaMP6f signal of three simultaneously modeled events (nose poke, lever presentation, lever press). To do this, we used kernels, or sets of regressors covering a series of time lags covering the period from 1 second before to 2 seconds after each event.
evidence: This describes the multiple event kernel analysis method.

claim: Each event had four kernels, corresponding to the four conditions from Figure 3a,c (all combinations of contralateral vs ipsilateral trials and previous reward vs no previous reward trials).
source: Each event had four kernels, corresponding to the four conditions from Figure 3a,c (all combinations of contralateral vs ipsilateral trials and previous reward vs no previous reward trials).
evidence: This describes the kernel analysis design.

claim: The kernels were solved by regressing the design matrix against GCaMP6f data using least squares in R with the rms package.
source: We solved for the kernels by regressing the design matrix against GCaMP6f data using least squares in R with the rms package (Harrell, 2018).
evidence: This describes the statistical method and software used.

claim: The standard error was calculated using rms' robcov (cluster robust-covariance) function to correct for violations of ordinary least squares assumptions due to animal-by-animal clustering in the residuals.
source: The standard error (colored fringes) was calculated using rms' robcov (cluster robust-covariance) function to correct for violations of ordinary least squares assumptions due to animal-by-animal clustering in the residuals.
evidence: This describes the statistical correction procedure.
